name: Heddle-loom weaving in the Andes
summary: Andean weavers took up the heddle loom around 1400 BCE; it sped up weaving greatly and let cloth making grow across the Andes.
description: A heddle lets the weaver work several sets of warp threads at once. The Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino dates heddle weaving in the Andes to around 1400 BCE and says that it streamlined weaving enormously and spurred the growth of the Andean textile industry. The museum gives no site or find for that date and does not say where the heddle came from.

impact.note: Scored on the general view and the museum's statement that the heddle spurred the growth of Andean textile making: loom-woven cloth became a main form of wealth and tribute across Andean societies for some three thousand years (reach 2, depth 2); generativity is lowered from the lead's 2 to 1 because the later Andean weaves are successors within the same craft and no descent beyond the Andes is known.

date.label: c. 1400 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino dates the development of heddle weaving in the Andes to around 1400 BCE.

evidence.supports: Around 1400 BCE, the development of heddle weaving allowed several warp thread systems to be used simultaneously, an important technological advance that streamlined the weaving process enormously and spurred the growth of the textile industry in the Andes.
evidence.locator: Paragraph on Andean weaving after the plain-weave description

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The museum's date of around 1400 BCE is later than the start of the Initial Period (about 1800 BCE), with which the heddle loom is usually associated, and the same paragraph puts wider cloth with multiple thread systems at La Galgada by around 2000 BCE; settle the date from Grieder 1984 on La Galgada, Doyon-Bernard's article on Peruvian weaving, or the Britannica Initial Period entry.
Find the sites and finds on which the date rests, so that the event can become dated archaeological evidence at a named place.
Verify the Huaca Prieta cotton cloth dates (the museum gives 3000 to 2200 BCE) and that those fabrics were twined rather than loom-woven.
Mesoamerican backstrap-loom weaving and its independence from the Andes were not assessed.

research.note: The source does not say where the heddle was developed or whether it was introduced from elsewhere, so independence is not established.
